Headers travel as Pub/Sub attributes, with no envelope of their own; an attribute that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. Every header of an outgoing message becomes an attribute of the Pub/Sub message, name and value unchanged. Each attribute of a delivery becomes a header, so a handler reads it with ctx.headers(). Attributes are text, so a header value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish with PubSubError::Publish instead of being rewritten. Pub/Sub accepts at most 100 attributes per message, names of up to 256 bytes and values of up to 1024 bytes, and refuses a message past them. Two headers have a meaning of their own. partition-key is the message's ordering key: it never travels as an attribute, and a delivery reports its ordering key under it. pubsub-delivery-attempt is the attempt number a delivery reports where the subscription counts attempts.

The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_headers.rs /// The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn ship( order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") { headers.insert("tenant", tenant.to_owned()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; match out.message(&shipment).with_headers(headers).publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_headers.rs /// The tenant arrives as an attribute of the order and leaves as an attribute of the shipment. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); if let Some(tenant) = ctx.headers().get_str("tenant") { headers.insert("tenant", tenant.to_owned()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

On a subscription with message ordering, messages that share an ordering key reach a subscriber in the order they were published. An ordering key is a string a publish carries, up to 1 KB. A subscription orders deliveries only when it was created with message ordering on, a setting that cannot change afterwards. A subscription create_with_topic creates has it on; one created elsewhere keeps its own setting. The order holds for messages of one key published to one region, so publishers of one key use the same locational endpoint. When a message of a key is redelivered, the messages published after it under that key come again too, acknowledged ones included. With a dead-letter policy on the subscription, the order may not hold. A publish names its key in one of three places, and the first one present wins. The ordering_key step, or a transform, writes it into the message's settings. The partition-key header is the portable spelling. The policy's default key applies where neither named one. A delivery reports the key it arrived under in the partition-key header.

Three events of one order, published under its key, arrive in that order. The test runs the same body in process and against the emulator. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering.rs /// The subscription `create_with_topic` creates has message ordering on, so the events of one /// order arrive in the order they were published. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("ordering-order-events-workers").create_with_topic("ordering-order-events") )] async fn track(event: &OrderEvent, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let key = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(event.order_id, event.step, key, "order event"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering.rs /// The subscription `create_with_topic` creates has message ordering on, so the events of one /// order arrive in the order they were published. struct Track; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for Track { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let key = ctx .headers() .get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) .unwrap_or_default(); tracing::info!(event.order_id, event.step, key, "order event"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn order_events() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("ordering-order-events-workers").create_with_topic("ordering-order-events") }

The ordering_key step names the ordering key of one publish, on the framework's publish builder. The step sits between message(..) and publish(), so the publish stays the mount site's: its codec, its transforms and its slot hold. It exists only on a builder over a Pub/Sub publisher. The handler bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>> and imports the prelude, which brings the PubSubOrdering trait. The key reaches the client as the message's own ordering key and never as an attribute. A key named by the call wins over the partition-key header and over the policy's key. A test reads the setting back with tb.out::<Slot>().with_options(..) and a PubSubPublishOptions value.

Each confirmation goes out under its order's key. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_key.rs /// Each confirmation goes out under its order's key, named on the call. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn confirm( order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let sent = out .message(&Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .to("confirmations") .ordering_key(format!("order-{}", order.id)) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_key.rs /// Each confirmation goes out under its order's key, named on the call. struct Confirm; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Confirm where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher<Options = PubSubPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .to("confirmations") .ordering_key(format!("order-{}", order.id)) .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

The partition-key header is the portable spelling of the ordering key, read on publish and written on every keyed delivery. A body that names no broker type sets the key through this header. On publish the header becomes the message's ordering key and does not travel as an attribute. The header names the same key as the in-memory broker's partition-key, so a service keeps its headers when it moves between the two. A key from the ordering_key step or a transform wins over the header, and the header wins over the policy's key. A value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. On a delivery the header holds the key the message was published under, and it is absent on a message without one.

The handler sets the header, and the shipment goes out under the order's key. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_header.rs /// The body names no broker type: the `partition-key` header orders the shipment. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn ship(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, format!("order-{}", order.id)); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = out .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .to("shipments") .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_header.rs /// The body names no broker type: the `partition-key` header orders the shipment. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, format!("order-{}", order.id)); let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id }; let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&shipment) .with_headers(headers) .to("shipments") .publish() .await; sent.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } }

Publish::default().ordering_key(..) orders every message of one mount site under one key, a reply included. The key belongs to the policy, so it applies to every publish of that slot or reply. A reply has no call site, so the policy is where a fixed key for replies goes. It suits a slot that belongs to one entity: one ledger, one device. A key named by the call or by the partition-key header wins over it. The AsyncAPI document reports the key in the message's binding.

Every ledger entry goes out under the key ledger. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_policy.rs /// Books every order in the ledger. #[subscriber("orders-workers", reply)] async fn book(order: &Order) -> LedgerEntry { LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // The ledger is one sequence, so every entry goes out under one key. b.include(book) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("ledger")); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_policy.rs /// Books every order in the ledger. struct Book; impl Handle<Order, LedgerEntry> for Book { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // The ledger is one sequence, so every entry goes out under one key. b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", Book).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default().ordering_key("ledger")); }, ) }

A reply transform over PubSubPublishOptions sets the reply's ordering key per delivery, read off the request. A reply has no call site, so a key that differs per reply is a transform's to write. The transform implements PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> and reads the delivery being answered. It writes the key into the message's settings, where the ordering_key step would. Naming the settings type ties the transform to Pub/Sub publishers: it mounts on no other broker. The mount site adds it after the reply policy with .transform(..).

Each receipt goes out under the key of the order it answers. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_publishing_ordering_transform.rs /// Sends each receipt under the key of the order it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(receipt) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_publishing_ordering_transform.rs /// Sends each receipt under the key of the order it answers, which the delivery reports in its /// `partition-key` header. struct ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey; impl<C> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, PubSubPublishOptions> for ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PubSubPublishOptions>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(key) = cx.headers().get_str(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER) { options .get_or_insert_with(PubSubPublishOptions::default) .ordering_key = Some(key.to_owned()); } } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", ReceiptFor).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish::default()) .transform(ReplyUnderTheOrdersKey); }, ) }

ack acknowledges a delivery, retry nacks it so Pub/Sub redelivers it, and drop acknowledges one that is not worth another attempt. Pub/Sub settles each message on its own, by acknowledging it or by giving it back. ack acknowledges, and the subscription does not deliver the message again. retry nacks, and the subscription redelivers the message, possibly to another consumer. A subscription with no retry policy redelivers at once; one with an exponential backoff policy waits first. drop acknowledges too: Pub/Sub has no verb that discards a message without settling it. The one exception is the last delivery a dead-letter policy allows: there drop nacks, so the service moves the message to the dead-letter topic. A delayed retry is retry_after.

A subscription with exactly-once delivery on guarantees that an acknowledged message is not delivered again. It is a property of the subscription's configuration, and the crate reads it off each delivery. On such a subscription an ack and a nack wait for the service to confirm them. An acknowledgement the service rejects, such as one whose lease has expired, fails the settlement with an AckError that carries the cause, and the message may come back. On other subscriptions an ack is sent in the background and returns at once. The guarantee holds for subscribers in the subscription's region, which a locational endpoint pins.

A reservation acknowledges an order it reserved, drops an order with nothing to reserve, and asks for another delivery while the stock is out. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement.rs /// Reserves stock for an order. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { // Nothing to reserve, now or later: acknowledged, never redelivered. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } if !order.in_stock { // Nacked: the subscription delivers the order again. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement.rs /// Reserves stock for an order. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.quantity == 0 { // Nothing to reserve, now or later: acknowledged, never redelivered. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } if !order.in_stock { // Nacked: the subscription delivers the order again. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, "stock reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } }

On a subscription with a dead-letter policy a delivery reports its attempt number in the pubsub-delivery-attempt header. Pub/Sub counts the deliveries of a message only where its subscription has a dead-letter policy. There each delivery carries the count, the first delivery being attempt 1, and the crate puts it in the header pubsub-delivery-attempt. A subscription without a policy reports no count, and the header is absent. A handler reads it with ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) and branches on it, for example to give a message up before the cap. The count is the service's estimate: it may miss a delivery, and it may start over from zero. The crate also reads it to tell the last allowed delivery, where drop nacks instead of acknowledging.

An order without stock waits through two redeliveries and is given up on the third attempt, before the cap of five. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_attempts.rs /// Waits for stock through two redeliveries, then gives the order up on the third attempt. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn reserve(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let attempt: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .and_then(|attempt| attempt.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if order.in_stock { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } if attempt >= 3 { tracing::error!(order.id, attempt, "no stock, order given up"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::warn!(order.id, attempt, "no stock yet"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_attempts.rs /// Waits for stock through two redeliveries, then gives the order up on the third attempt. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let attempt: u32 = ctx .headers() .get_str(DELIVERY_ATTEMPT_HEADER) .and_then(|attempt| attempt.parse().ok()) .unwrap_or(1); if order.in_stock { return ready(Ok(())); } if attempt >= 3 { tracing::error!(order.id, attempt, "no stock, order given up"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::warn!(order.id, attempt, "no stock yet"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } }

max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(topic) at the mount site become the subscription's own dead-letter policy, written at startup. A Pub/Sub subscription moves a spent message itself. After n deliveries the service stops redelivering the message and publishes it to the dead-letter topic, with its payload and its attributes. The crate publishes nothing: it writes the declaration onto the subscription as its dead-letter policy. A subscription that create_with_topic creates carries the policy from the start, and the dead-letter topic is created with it. A subscription that already exists gets the policy written onto it at startup, whether the handler names it by string or by descriptor. The policy is one field of the subscription with both halves, so the mount site declares both. A cap without a topic, a topic without a cap, or a cap outside the 5 to 100 Pub/Sub accepts fails the startup. Two registrations on one subscription that declare different policies fail the startup too. .out_retry(..) does not compile on this broker, because no retry copy is ever published. The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, read through a subscription of its own. A message published to a topic with no subscription is lost, so the reader's subscription exists before the first message is spent. The Pub/Sub service account of the project needs permission to publish to the dead-letter topic and to subscribe to the source subscription. Pub/Sub counts deliveries on a best-effort basis, so a message may get a few more or fewer than n.

Five deliveries of a declined payment; after the fifth, Pub/Sub publishes it to payments-dead. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_dead_letters.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment; after the fifth Pub/Sub publishes it to // `payments-dead`, payload and attributes as they arrived. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); b.include(on_dead_letter); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_dead_letters.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment; after the fifth Pub/Sub publishes it to // `payments-dead`, payload and attributes as they arrived. b.include(subscriber(payments(), Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments-dead"); b.include(subscriber(dead_letters(), OnDeadLetter).build()); }, ) } The dead-letter topic is read by an ordinary subscription: Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_dead_letters.rs /// The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, read through a subscription of its own. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("payments-dead-audit").create_with_topic("payments-dead"))] async fn on_dead_letter(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment dead-lettered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_dead_letters.rs /// The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, read through a subscription of its own. struct OnDeadLetter; impl Handle<Payment> for OnDeadLetter { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment dead-lettered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn dead_letters() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("payments-dead-audit").create_with_topic("payments-dead") }

retry_after(delay) holds the delivery under its lease for the delay, then nacks it, so the subscription redelivers it once the delay is over. Pub/Sub has no delayed nack, so the crate keeps the delivery in the process for the delay. The client goes on extending the delivery's lease while it waits, so the service does not redeliver it early. The wait runs on a task of its own, and the subscription keeps delivering meanwhile. The held delivery counts toward max_outstanding until it comes back, and its redelivery counts as an attempt toward a dead-letter policy. Nothing is published: the message itself comes back, with its payload and its attributes, and with the next attempt number where the subscription counts attempts. The delay must fit inside the subscription's max_lease, an hour by default. A longer one is refused with PubSubError::DelayBeyondLease, and the delivery comes back at once. A process that stops while it holds a delivery stops extending its lease, and the service redelivers the message when the lease runs out: the delay is lost, the message is not.

A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds. The test advances the paused clock and sees the second delivery only once the thirty seconds are over. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds, not at once. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("payments-workers").create_with_topic("payments"))] async fn reconcile(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if !payment.settled { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment reconciled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_settlement_retry_after.rs /// A payment the bank has not settled yet comes back in thirty seconds, not at once. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Payment> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !payment.settled { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment reconciled"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A name in #[subscriber] reads that existing Pub/Sub subscription; the GooglePubSub descriptor carries every other setting of one. Pub/Sub keeps topics and subscriptions apart. A publisher sends to a topic, and a subscription attached to the topic keeps every message published after it was created. Each subscription of a topic receives every message, and the consumers of one subscription share its messages. A service reads a subscription, never a topic. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] reads the subscription orders-workers, which the deployment created on its topic. The name is a short id in the broker's project or a full resource name, projects/{project}/subscriptions/{id}. Nothing is created at startup, and a subscription that does not exist fails on its stream with PubSubError::Receive. A dead-letter declaration at the mount site reaches a subscription named this way too. Every other setting belongs to the descriptor, which goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor goes in the same place, subscriber(descriptor, body). Two handlers on one subscription are two consumers of it: each message goes to one of them.

The subscription orders-workers of the project my-project. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`, which the deployment created on its topic. #[subscriber("orders-workers")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(place); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions.rs /// Reads the subscription `orders-workers`, which the deployment created on its topic. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders-workers", Place).build()); }, ) }

ack_extension sets how far each background extension of a delivery's lease reaches, from 10 seconds to 10 minutes, 60 seconds by default. Pub/Sub redelivers a message whose ack deadline passes before it is settled. While a handler works, the client library extends that deadline in the background, each time by this much. A longer extension means fewer calls for a slow handler. A shorter one brings a delivery back sooner when the process dies, because the service redelivers once the last extension runs out. The client clamps the value to the 10 seconds to 10 minutes Pub/Sub accepts. It is independent of the ack deadline configured on the subscription. How long the client keeps extending one delivery is max_lease.

A report takes minutes to render, so each extension reaches five minutes. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// A report takes minutes to render, so each extension of its lease reaches five minutes. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-reports-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-reports") .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(5)) )] async fn render(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(report.id, "report rendered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// A report takes minutes to render, so each extension of its lease reaches five minutes. fn reports() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-reports-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-reports") .ack_extension(Duration::from_mins(5)) }

A slice handler takes batches assembled on the client: batch(n) bounds their size, and batch_wait the wait for a partial one. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The streaming pull hands over one delivery at a time, so the subscription gathers deliveries into a batch itself. A batch goes to the handler when it holds n deliveries, or when batch_wait has passed since its first one, 50 milliseconds by default. So a quiet subscription yields small batches, and a busy one full ones. One outcome settles every delivery of the batch; a Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles delivery i with outcome i. Every delivery of a batch is outstanding while the batch waits, so max_outstanding below n keeps batches short of n. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles delivery by delivery.

Three orders published together arrive in one call. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_batches.rs /// The slice makes this a batch handler; a partial batch waits 200 milliseconds for the rest. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)))] async fn settle(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // At most 50 orders reach the handler per call. b.include(settle.batch(nonzero!(50))); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_batches.rs /// The slice makes this a batch handler; a partial batch waits 200 milliseconds for the rest. struct Settle; impl Handle<[Order]> for Settle { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { // At most 50 orders reach the handler per call. b.include( subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(200)), Settle, ) .batch(nonzero!(50)) .build(), ); }, ) }

create_with_topic creates the subscription and its topic at startup where they are missing, with message ordering on. At startup the subscription looks the topic up and creates it when it is missing. It does the same for the declared dead-letter topic, and then for the subscription itself, attached to the topic. A subscription it creates has message ordering on and carries the declared dead-letter policy. A subscription that already exists keeps its own configuration; the crate changes only its dead-letter policy, where the mount site declared one. The calls need the permissions to create topics and subscriptions, which a production service often lacks. So the step suits the emulator, tests and services that own their topology; elsewhere the topology is infrastructure and the descriptor only names it. Several subscriptions created on one topic each receive every message published to it.

Two subscriptions on the topic orders: each receives every order. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) )] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// A second subscription on the same topic: it receives every order too. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub::new("orders-audit").create_with_topic("orders"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) } /// A second subscription on the same topic: it receives every order too. fn audit() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-audit").create_with_topic("orders") }

GooglePubSub names one subscription by short id or full resource name and carries its settings: topology, flow control, leases and batches. GooglePubSub::new takes the subscription's name, and builder steps add the rest. create_with_topic creates the subscription and its topic at startup. max_outstanding caps the deliveries that may be unsettled at once. ack_extension and max_lease shape how the client keeps a delivery leased. batch_wait bounds how long a partial batch waits for the rest. A setting the descriptor leaves out keeps the client library's default. The descriptor is plain data and holds no connection. It opens against the connected broker at startup, so the declaration a service ships is the one its tests run.

The subscription orders-workers on the topic orders, with at most 100 orders unsettled at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) )] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// The subscription `orders-workers` on the topic `orders`, with at most 100 orders unsettled. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("orders-workers") .create_with_topic("orders") .max_outstanding(100) }

max_lease is how long the client keeps extending the lease of one unsettled delivery, an hour by default, and the budget of retry_after. After a delivery has been held this long, the client stops extending its lease. The lease then runs out, and Pub/Sub redelivers the message, possibly to another consumer. A handler that may run longer than an hour needs a longer lease. retry_after(delay) holds the delivery in the process for the delay, under this same lease. A delay longer than max_lease is refused with PubSubError::DelayBeyondLease, and the delivery comes back at once. The refusal keeps the delivery from coming back before the delay is over, from a lease that ran out.

An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. The tests advance the clock past the ninety minutes, and show that a delay of three hours comes back at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-invoices-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-invoices") .max_lease(Duration::from_hours(2)) )] async fn send(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { if !invoice.ready { return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(NOT_READY); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice sent"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// An invoice that is not ready comes back in ninety minutes, inside a lease of two hours. struct Send; impl Handle<Invoice> for Send { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !invoice.ready { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(NOT_READY))); } tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice sent"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn invoices() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-invoices-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-invoices") .max_lease(Duration::from_hours(2)) }

max_outstanding caps how many deliveries may be unsettled at once; Pub/Sub stops sending at the cap and resumes below it. A delivery is outstanding from the moment the service receives it until a handler settles it. The limit travels with the streaming pull, and the service holds the stream to it. It applies to one stream, not to the subscription as a whole: two instances of the service each hold their own share. The default is the client library's 1000 messages; a value of zero or less sets no limit. A delivery held by retry_after stays outstanding until it comes back. The client also caps outstanding bytes at 100 MiB, a limit the descriptor leaves at its default.

At most 50 orders are unsettled at once. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// At most 50 orders are unsettled at once; the service holds the rest back. #[subscriber( GooglePubSub::new("flow-orders-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-orders") .max_outstanding(50) )] async fn index(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order indexed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_flow.rs /// At most 50 orders are unsettled at once; the service holds the rest back. fn orders() -> GooglePubSub { GooglePubSub::new("flow-orders-workers") .create_with_topic("flow-orders") .max_outstanding(50) }

#[subscriber(GooglePubSub)] fixes the kind of subscription, and name at the mount site leaves its name to the deployment. A handler written with the bare kind has no subscription yet. .name("orders-workers") where it is mounted builds the descriptor, as GooglePubSub::new would. A definition mounted without a name does not compile. The descriptor built this way keeps every default; a subscription with settings of its own is a descriptor in the attribute. The same handler serves several deployments that each read a subscription of their own, such as one per region. The manual form starts from Unnamed::<GooglePubSub>::new() and takes the same .name(..) step.

Each deployment names its subscription in ORDERS_SUBSCRIPTION. Macros Manual examples/pubsub_subscriptions_name.rs /// A Pub/Sub subscription whose name the deployment decides. #[subscriber(GooglePubSub)] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// One service per region, each reading the subscription of its region. fn service(subscription: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include(place.name(subscription)); }, ) } examples/manual/pubsub_subscriptions_name.rs /// A Pub/Sub subscription whose name the deployment decides. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// One service per region, each reading the subscription of its region. fn service(subscription: String) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PubSubBroker::new("my-project"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(Unnamed::<GooglePubSub>::new(), Place) .name(subscription) .build(), ); }, ) }

TestApp::start connects PubSubBroker in process: topics, subscriptions, redelivery and dead letters, with no emulator. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PubSubBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. Nothing is dialled and no credentials are read, so a test runs where the service could not authenticate. The in-process mode keeps Pub/Sub's model. A topic and a subscription are separate, and a subscription receives every message published to its topic after it was created, whether or not a consumer is open. A subscription the service only names is taken to exist, attached to the topic of its own name; create_with_topic attaches one to the topic it names. The consumers of one subscription share its messages in turn. A nack redelivers, a retry_after waits on the test's clock, and a dead-letter policy counts attempts and moves a spent message. It refuses what the service refuses: a resource name it does not accept, an empty message, an attribute or an ordering key past its limits or not UTF-8. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled. With tokio::time::pause(), or #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)], tb.advance(d) moves the clock and runs what fell due. Leases, flow control, ordered delivery by key and exactly-once delivery belong to the service; a live test checks them against the emulator.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-gcp-pubsub = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against the Pub/Sub emulator, for leases, flow control and ordered delivery. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so every subscription opens a real streaming pull. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live app is the production one on a broker pointed at the emulator. The emulator starts empty, so its subscriptions create themselves with create_with_topic. It keeps its subscriptions until it stops, so a run that failed can leave messages behind for the next one. The examples delete their subscriptions before each live run, which live::fresh does with the client library's admin API. In the example, live::host returns the emulator's address from PUBSUB_TEST_HOST, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no emulator. A job that stood an emulator up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the emulator at PUBSUB_TEST_HOST.
